## Description

<p>You are given the <code>root</code> of a binary tree.</p>
<p>A ZigZag path for a binary tree is defined as follow:</p>
<ul>
	<li>Choose <strong>any </strong>node in the binary tree and a direction (right or left).</li>
	<li>If the current direction is right, move to the right child of the current node; otherwise, move to the left child.</li>
	<li>Change the direction from right to left or from left to right.</li>
	<li>Repeat the second and third steps until you can&#39;t move in the tree.</li>
</ul>
<p>Zigzag length is defined as the number of nodes visited - 1. (A single node has a length of 0).</p>
<p>Return <em>the longest <strong>ZigZag</strong> path contained in that tree</em>.</p>
<p><strong class="example">Example 1:</strong></p>

![[Personal/LeetCode/Assets/LetCode Assets/longest-zigzag-path-in-a-binary-tree_0.png]]
<pre>
<strong>Input:</strong> root = [1,null,1,1,1,null,null,1,1,null,1,null,null,null,1]
<strong>Output:</strong> 3
<strong>Explanation:</strong> Longest ZigZag path in blue nodes (right -&gt; left -&gt; right).
</pre>
<p><strong class="example">Example 2:</strong></p>

![[Personal/LeetCode/Assets/LetCode Assets/longest-zigzag-path-in-a-binary-tree_1.png]]
<pre>
<strong>Input:</strong> root = [1,1,1,null,1,null,null,1,1,null,1]
<strong>Output:</strong> 4
<strong>Explanation:</strong> Longest ZigZag path in blue nodes (left -&gt; right -&gt; left -&gt; right).
</pre>
<p><strong class="example">Example 3:</strong></p>
<pre>
<strong>Input:</strong> root = [1]
<strong>Output:</strong> 0
</pre>
<p><strong>Constraints:</strong></p>
<ul>
	<li>The number of nodes in the tree is in the range <code>[1, 5 * 10<sup>4</sup>]</code>.</li>
	<li><code>1 &lt;= Node.val &lt;= 100</code></li>
</ul>

# Solution

The first solution that comes to my mind is to implement a DFS brute force. We start from the root and go down with DFS, and at each node, we start another DFS to find the maximum zig-zag path starting from that node. We keep a global max value and update it whenever we find a longer zig-zag.

$N + (N - 1) + (N - 2) + ... + 1 = O(N²)$

This is a very expensive operation, especially for skewed trees.
Let’s go ahead and implement this brute-force approach first.

```python
from algos.binarytree import Node


def longest_zigzag_path_in_bt(root: Node) -> int:
	ans = 0
	
	def dfs(root: Node, go_left: bool, lenght: int):
		nonlocal ans
		
		ans = max(ans, lenght)
		
		if go_left:
			dfs(root.left, False, lenght + 1)
			dfs(root.right, True, 1)
		else:
			dfs(root.right, True, length + 1)
			dfs(root.left, False, 1)

	dfs(node.left, False, 1)
	dfs(node.right, True, 1)
	return ans
	

root = Node.create_binarytree([1,None,1,1,1,None,None,1,1,None,1,None,None,None,1])
print(longest_zigzag_path(root))

root = Node.create_binarytree([1,1,1,None,1,None,None,1,1,None,1])
print(longest_zigzag_path(root))

root = Node.create_binarytree([1])
print(longest_zigzag_path(root))
```


## Optimization

Now that we solved it with brute force, how can we improve the algorithm to only traverse the tree once. Let's think about state at each node. Starting from the root node we do not have any zig-zag yet, since we haven’t taken any edge. So let's dive into the children. After taking the first edge, we have a zig-zag of length 1, but we still don’t know if it will continue.

Now, if we want to extend a zig-zag, we need to know where the previous node came from. Was it from the left side of the parent? Then the next move must be to the right to continue the zig-zag. If that happens, we can increase the zig-zag length by one.

If instead we go in the same direction again, the zig-zag breaks and we reset the length back to 1 (since a single edge is still a valid zig-zag).

So at each node, we only need to keep track of two states: the longest zig-zag ending at this node when the last move was to the left, and the longest zig-zag ending at this node when the last move was to the right.

<div>
<div class="excalidraw-svg excalidraw-dark" style="background-image:url(data:image/svg+xml;base64,);background-size:cover;background-repeat:no-repeat;width:356.6307067871094px;height:auto;aspect-ratio:0.8491426337567272;"></div>
<div class="excalidraw-svg excalidraw-light" style="background-image:url(data:image/svg+xml;base64,);background-size:cover;background-repeat:no-repeat;width:356.6307067871094px;height:auto;aspect-ratio:0.8491426337567272;"></div>
</div>
The example above shows how we can increment the zigzag count of (left, right) from bottom up.

This way, we can compute the answer in a single DFS traversal. Let's implement it.

```python
def longest_zigzag_path(root: Node):
	ans = 0
	
	def dfs(node: Node) -> tuple[int, int]:
		nonlocal ans
		if not node: return 0, 0 
		
		left_len = right_len = 0

		if node.left:
			_, right_len = dfs(node.left)
			left_len = right_len + 1
		else:
			left_len, _ = dfs(node.right)
			right_len = left_len + 1
			
		return left_len, right_len
	
	left, right = dfs(root)
	return max(left, right)

root = Node.create_binarytree([1,None,1,1,1,None,None,1,1,None,1,None,None,None,1])
print(longest_zigzag_path(root))

root = Node.create_binarytree([1,1,1,None,1,None,None,1,1,None,1])
print(longest_zigzag_path(root))

root = Node.create_binarytree([1])
print(longest_zigzag_path(root))
```
